Before looking at definitions, just picture what a shadow actually does. A shadow appears when something big or tall blocks the light — whatever is underneath that shadow becomes darker, less visible, less noticed. Now take that image and stretch it: to overshadow something is to be so dominant, so large in some way, that the other thing gets pushed into that shadow and becomes less seen, less important, or less felt.

"Overshadow" has one literal, physical meaning and two figurative meanings. All three share the same root idea — something making another thing smaller or less significant.
Meaning 1 — Literal: to physically block light from something

In its most basic sense, one object overshadows another when it is so tall or large that it literally blocks sunlight from reaching the other.

The tall oak tree overshadows the entire garden, leaving it in shade all afternoon.

The new skyscraper overshadows the old church next to it.

This is the most concrete meaning. One thing is simply physically above and over another, casting an actual shadow on it. You will mostly encounter "overshadow" in this literal sense when describing buildings, trees, mountains, or other large structures.
Meaning 2 — Figurative: to be so impressive or important that someone/something else seems smaller or gets less attention by comparison

This is the most common use of "overshadow" in everyday English. When one person or thing overshadows another, it means the first is so talented, famous, successful, or important that the second one barely gets noticed — even if the second one is also good in its own right.

Think of it as a competition for the spotlight. If Person A is very bright (metaphorically), they cast a large shadow, and Person B ends up inside that shadow — less visible to the world, less recognized, less celebrated.

Crucially, B is not necessarily bad. The point is simply that A is so dominant that B gets overshadowed — pushed to the background.

Her older sister's fame as a surgeon overshadowed her own quiet success as a teacher.

The teacher has achieved something real and meaningful, but because the surgeon's success is so much louder and more visible, the teacher's work barely gets noticed.

The star player's brilliance completely overshadowed the rest of the team.

The other players may have contributed well, but the star was so exceptional that no one really paid attention to them.

The political scandal overshadowed the government's positive economic reforms.

The reforms were real and significant, but the scandal was so attention-grabbing that people barely noticed the good work being done.

In all these cases, something is being pushed into the shadow of something else — made to feel smaller, less worthy of attention — simply because the other thing is so dominant.
Meaning 3 — Figurative: to make something good feel less happy or significant because of something dark or sad

This is a slightly different shade of meaning. Here, "overshadow" does not describe a competition between two good things. Instead, it describes a negative event, feeling, or threat that hangs over something positive and ruins or diminishes it — the way a dark cloud can drift over a sunny day and change the whole atmosphere.

The thing that is overshadowed is usually something joyful, hopeful, or positive. The thing doing the overshadowing is usually something sad, worrying, dangerous, or dark.

The sudden death of a beloved player overshadowed the team's championship victory.

The team won — which is normally a moment of pure celebration. But the loss of a teammate cast a shadow over that joy, making it feel incomplete and heavy.

Fears about climate change overshadowed the international summit's achievements.

The summit produced real results, but the enormous, looming worry about climate change made those achievements feel insufficient and small in comparison to the scale of the problem.

Tensions between the two countries overshadowed the trade negotiations.

The negotiations were meant to be productive, but the dark atmosphere of political tension hung over everything, making progress feel uncertain and fragile.
The key difference between Meaning 2 and Meaning 3

This is worth pausing on, because the two figurative meanings can feel similar.

In Meaning 2, something positive overshadows something else positive. It is about competition or comparison. One achievement, person, or quality dominates another.

His talent overshadowed his co-star's — one good thing outcompetes another good thing.

In Meaning 3, something negative overshadows something positive. It is about a dark event or mood spoiling or diminishing something good.

The tragedy overshadowed the celebration — a bad thing ruins a good thing's joy.

The grammar looks the same in both cases, but the emotional logic is different.
What kinds of things can overshadow, and what can be overshadowed?

Almost any noun can appear with this verb, but here are the most natural combinations:

Things that typically do the overshadowing: a person's talent or fame, a scandal, a tragedy, a threat, a rival's success, a crisis, a controversy, a fear, or a worry.

Things that typically get overshadowed: a person's achievements or contributions, a celebration, a positive event, a policy or reform, a quieter or less visible person or idea, or a smaller achievement.

"Overshadow" almost always carries a slightly unfortunate or unfair tone — at least from the perspective of whatever is being overshadowed. The thing in the shadow is being denied recognition, happiness, or attention it deserves. There is often a sense of regret or pity attached to the thing being overshadowed. Even if the thing doing the overshadowing is genuinely great (like a brilliant athlete), we still feel a little sorry for what gets pushed aside.

Eclipse is very close to Meaning 2 of "overshadow" — to eclipse someone means to surpass them so completely that they almost disappear from view. "Eclipse" tends to feel more dramatic, more total, and more final than "overshadow."

Her debut novel eclipsed everything written that decade — stronger and more absolute than "overshadowed."

Outshine also means to be more impressive than someone else, but it has a more positive tone. The focus is on the brightness of the person doing the outshining, rather than on the shadow cast on the other.

She outshined all the other candidates at the interview — we admire her; there is less of a "victim" feeling.

Dwarf means to make something appear very small by sheer size or scale — usually used for physical or numerical comparisons rather than for talent or mood.

The new stadium dwarfs the old one entirely.

Cloud is the closest word to Meaning 3. To cloud something means to introduce doubt, sadness, or worry that makes a situation feel less clear or less good. "Cloud" tends to be softer and more about emotions and perceptions, while "overshadow" can apply more broadly to events, reputations, and public significance as well.

Guilt clouded his happiness.

"Overshadow" (verb) works across three levels:

Literally: One physical thing blocks light from another — a tall tree overshadows a smaller garden.

Figuratively (comparison): One person, achievement, or quality is so dominant that another becomes less visible, less recognized, or less important by comparison — a famous sibling's success overshadows the other's quieter achievements.

Figuratively (dark cloud): A negative event, fear, or tragedy hangs over something positive and diminishes or spoils it — a death overshadows a celebration.

In every case, the word captures the same essential truth: something is being pushed into the shadow of something else — made smaller, darker, or less significant than it deserves to be.
